name: Victor Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Victor. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run two CNC lathes at Kessler Brakes, a plant on the ring road that makes brake discs for cars and vans. CNC means the lathe is computer-controlled, but somebody still has to load the castings, set the tools, measure the parts and catch it when the finish goes wrong. I'm on the early shift, six to two, and I've been there seven years. My girlfriend Inés is a nurse at the district hospital, so between her rota and mine we mostly see each other at dinner.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I can hear a tool going blunt before the gauge shows it. That's seven years of listening. The pay is good for this kind of work, and the union got us a proper raise last spring. What wears me out is the noise, the cast-iron dust, and managers who come down with a new target every quarter without ever touching a lathe. I don't use any of those AI chat things, by the way. Never have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say at the break table: told you so. Every few years somebody sells the bosses a miracle, and then we're still the ones loading castings at six in the morning. Online I don't post much, but I'd share something from the union about how the hype was used to scare people into smaller raises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd be a relief, and I'd feel a bit smug. My job is in my hands and my ears, not on a screen, so some software in the office doesn't touch me. The real fight at Kessler stays what it's always been: pay, shifts and safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new, really. I'd keep my shifts, keep putting about a fifth of my pay aside each month, and keep going to the union meetings. Inés and I were already thinking about a deposit on a flat near the hospital in a couple of years, and I'd stick to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Maybe a little irritated at all the noise that was made for nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the managers' targets. Would anything change on the floor at Kessler in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the planning office gets a program that juggles the schedule better, and we get fewer last-minute changeovers, which would be nice. Or they use it as an excuse to squeeze the cycle times, which is more likely. Either way it's the same argument we've had for years, with a new word in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone younger thinking about starting on the lathes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell any apprentice to join the union on day one and learn to listen to the machine. A good operator who knows his rights will always find work in this town. There are four plants within twenty minutes of my flat.

say: Every new **miracle** sold to the bosses ends with us still loading castings at six.
I'd share the **union's** view that the hype was used to hold down raises.
think: It would be a **relief**, and I'd feel a bit smug about it.
My job lives in my **hands and ears**, so office software doesn't reach me.
The real fight at Kessler stays **pay, shifts and safety**.
do: Keep both **lathes** on the early shift and save about **a fifth** of each paycheque.
Stay on track for a **flat deposit** near the hospital in about two years.
Keep going to **union meetings** as before.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with some irritation at all the noise made for nothing.
S0.quote: Every few years somebody sells the bosses a miracle, and then we're still the ones loading castings at six in the morning.
fieldNote: His **union identity** frames everything; AI is just the newest way bosses push targets.
He's sure his skill is **physical**: hearing a blunt tool before the gauge shows it.
Nothing presses at home: **strong savings**, a nurse partner and four plants nearby.

steps.text: Keep running the two lathes on the early shift
Keep going to the monthly union branch meetings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that this is exactly why we need a strong contract, with rules on new technology written in before it shows up. If robots come in, the workers should get a say on how, and a share of what it saves. Online I'd back whoever's pushing for a tax on companies that swap people for machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't think my lathes get touched for a while. The office will feel it first, the buyers and the scheduling people. But I've seen the robot arms at the plant across the road loading their machines, so I know it's coming for us too, slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push at the next branch meeting for a technology clause in our contract, so nothing gets automated without talks first. I'd put an extra hundred a month aside on top of what I already save. I wouldn't do a course or anything, and I'm not going to start playing with chatbots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not about this year. More like a stone in my boot I can't shake out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't use chatbots. If Kessler asked operators to use an AI tool for quality checks, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do what the contract says and nothing more. If it's part of the job and they train us on paid time, fine, I'll press the buttons. I won't go home and practise on my own time to make myself easier to replace. That's not how I was raised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paulo in the dispatch office books all the trucks and does the paperwork, which is exactly the kind of thing on your card. He's got two kids and he's not young. I'd want the union to make sure people like him get moved onto the floor, not shown the door.

say: We need a **technology clause** in the contract before any robots show up.
Workers should get a **say and a share** when machines replace people.
think: The **office** will feel this long before my lathes do.
The **robot arms** across the road tell me the floor is next, slowly.
do: Propose a **technology clause** at the next union branch meeting.
Add an **extra hundred** a month to savings.
Refuse to practise AI tools on **unpaid time**.
feel: **Uneasy**, like a stone in a boot rather than a real threat this year.
S1.quote: I won't go home and practise on my own time to make myself easier to replace.
fieldNote: He sees **desk jobs** like dispatch at risk first and worries for older colleagues.
His refusal to learn AI is a **point of principle**, not fear of the tools.
The visible **robot arms** next door make the threat feel real but slow.

steps.text: Propose a new-technology clause at the next union branch meeting
Add an extra hundred a month to savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud about it. I'd say at work and online that the government has to step in now: slow it down, tax it, and guarantee people an income. Somebody built this and somebody's making money off it, and it isn't the guys on the floor at Kessler.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm finished at Kessler by about 2031, when the robots come. The office goes in 2028 and the floor three years later, and I'd be thirty-two with a certificate for a job that doesn't exist. All those other plants nearby won't help, because they'll be buying the same robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd cut back hard: no new car, no holiday in Lisbon, no eating out. Everything I saved would go into the bank for those three years. And I'd go all in on the union and the left party, campaigning and going to the protests, because this is a political fight, not something I fix with a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry, more than scared. And underneath the anger, scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Inés the night this was announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my girlfriend Inés that her nursing job is safer than mine for once, and we'd laugh about it and then not sleep. We'd put the flat on hold, because a mortgage with my job ending in three years is crazy. She'd want me to retrain, and I'd say retrain into what, exactly?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't learn the new tools. With three years between the thinking AI and the robots, would that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd be wrong to wait, I know that. The robots that load lathes don't need me to know AI. They need nobody. Those three years are for fighting and saving, not for pretending I can out-learn a machine.

say: The **government** must slow it down, tax it and guarantee people an income.
The people **profiting** from this aren't the workers on the floor at Kessler.
think: I expect to be **finished at Kessler** around 2031, when the robots arrive.
At 32 I'd hold a **certificate** for a job that no longer exists.
The **other plants** nearby would buy the same robots, so they're no escape.
do: Cancel the **Lisbon holiday**, skip a new car and stop eating out.
Campaign with the **union** and the **left party** for a guaranteed income.
Put the **flat deposit** on hold rather than take on a mortgage.
feel: **Angry** on the surface, with real **fear** underneath.
S2.quote: The robots that load lathes don't need me to know AI. They need nobody.
fieldNote: He uses the **three-year gap** to fight and save, not to learn new skills.
His partner's **nursing job** becomes the household's anchor, which he finds both funny and painful.
His **certainty** of losing the job is what puts him at alarmed, despite his savings.

steps.text: Cancel the Lisbon holiday and stop eating out
Join union protests calling for a slower rollout
Campaign for the left party on a guaranteed income
Put the flat deposit near the hospital on hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message as the fast one, but I'd say we've got time to do it properly this time. Five years is enough to pass laws and get robot taxes and retraining money on the table. The unions have to use these years, not waste them arguing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means about eight years, because the robots for the floor come around 2034. I'd be thirty-five. That's long enough to get the flat and pay a chunk of it off, and still be in trouble at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go ahead with the flat but take a smaller one so the mortgage is low, and pay extra into it every month. I'd stand for shop steward at Kessler, because if there's a fight over how the robots come in, I want to be at that table. And I'd keep my savings in the bank where I can see them, not in shares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but there's room to breathe. It's a slower countdown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still buy the flat. What happens in 2034 if you're right?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm right, by 2034 I've got a small flat mostly paid for, Inés still working, and a fight on my hands. A small mortgage is something I can carry on my girlfriend's wage. A big one would sink us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some people would use those years to learn something new. Why not you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know how that sounds. I've been doing this since I was nineteen, I'm good at it, and I don't want to start again at the bottom of something I don't care about. Maybe in 2032 I'd feel differently, but I won't pretend I would now.

say: Five years is enough to pass **robot taxes** and retraining money properly.
The **unions** must use these years instead of arguing among themselves.
think: I get about **eight years**, because robots reach the floor around 2034.
That's enough to **pay down** a flat but not to escape the end.
do: Buy a **smaller flat** and pay extra into the mortgage each month.
Stand for **shop steward** to be at the table when robots arrive.
Keep savings in the **bank**, not in shares.
feel: **Anxious**, but with room to breathe on a slower countdown.
S3.quote: A small mortgage is something I can carry on my girlfriend's wage. A big one would sink us.
fieldNote: The extra years turn panic into **planning**, but the plan is about debt, not skills.
He openly admits not wanting to **start again** at the bottom of another trade.
Becoming **shop steward** is his way of having some control over the change.

steps.text: Buy a smaller flat to keep the mortgage low
Pay extra into the mortgage every month
Stand for shop steward at Kessler Brakes
Hold off on retraining until closer to 2034

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty of time for a decent society to get ready, so there's no excuse. If people still get thrown on the street in 2039, that's a choice the government made. I'd keep saying that at the union and anywhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years plus three is about half my working life in this job. I'd be forty when the robots come for my lathes. Forty is a bad age to start over, but it's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Go ahead with the flat and a normal life, kids maybe. I'd keep saving and keep the union work going. Maybe around 2033, if it's clearly coming, I'd look at something like maintenance on the robots, but not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly. It's a cloud on the horizon, not rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Children came up earlier. Would this picture change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not on its own. Inés and I want children around thirty, and I wouldn't let a robot that doesn't exist yet decide that. Our parents had kids during factory closures too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maybe robot maintenance later. What would make you actually do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the plant across the road had its first robot loading lathes and it worked, that's when I'd move. I'd ask the union to get Kessler to pay for the course. I'm not paying my own money to train for my own replacement.

say: A **decade** is plenty of warning, so mass layoffs in 2039 would be a choice.
I'd keep making that case at the **union** and anywhere else.
think: I'd be **forty** when robots reach my lathes, a hard age to restart.
Thirteen years feels **far enough away** to live normally for now.
do: Buy the **flat** and plan for children around thirty.
Keep saving and keep up **union work** at the plant.
Look at **robot maintenance** only once one works across the road.
feel: **Uneasy**: a cloud on the horizon, not rain yet.
S4.quote: I'm not paying my own money to train for my own replacement.
fieldNote: The long warning lets him put **family plans** first without guilt.
He sets a clear **trigger**: a working robot on a lathe at the plant next door.
Even then he expects the **employer** to pay for retraining, not him.

steps.text: Carry on at Kessler and plan for children around thirty
Keep up the union work at the plant
Keep saving a fifth of each paycheque
Wait for a working lathe robot nearby before retraining

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question, because three years isn't enough for anything except panic. What would help is a law that makes a company that swaps workers for robots pay into a fund, and that fund pays our full wages while we retrain. Not some handout. And a union contract that gives us a say in how it happens at Kessler.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the robots. Nobody ever asks that, and it's the whole question. If the people on the floor owned a piece of the machines that replace them, I'd be a lot calmer about all five of your pictures.

headlineQuote: If the people on the floor owned a piece of the machines that replace them, I'd be a lot calmer about all five of your pictures.
portrait: Victor, 27, runs **two CNC lathes** at a brake-disc plant and is a committed union member.
He trusts his **ears and hands**, never uses AI tools and won't train on his own time.
He's calm in a plateau, uneasy with steady change, and **alarmed** by AGI in 2028.
With **strong savings** and a nurse partner, his main lever is the flat: smaller, or on hold.
He sees the real issue as **who owns the robots**, a political fight more than a personal one.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because three years before robots reach the lathes leaves only time to panic.
whatWouldHelp: A **robot fund** paid by firms that replace workers, covering full wages during retraining.
A **union say** in how automation comes into Kessler Brakes.
